index_record.dataset_generation_caption:
The figure illustrates a neural network architecture designed to predict postoperative facial appearance from a preoperative 3D scan. The global layout is a left-to-right pipeline, starting with input data on the far left and progressing through several processing modules to produce a reconstructed 3D mesh on the right, with feedback loops and loss computation indicated by dashed lines. The entire process is divided into two phases: training (including all components) and testing (excluding the dashed-line components).

On the left, two inputs are shown: a 3D scan of a face and a set of facial landmarks marked with red dots. These inputs are fed into a trapezoidal module labeled 'FLAME fitting', which processes them to generate a compact representation called the 'latent code'. This latent code is represented as a blue vertical cylinder.

The latent code is then passed to a rectangular box labeled 'code difference predictor', which computes a 'code diff'—represented as an orange vertical cylinder. This code diff is added to the original latent code via a circular '+' node, producing a 'predicted code'—shown as a purple vertical cylinder.

The predicted code is then fed into another trapezoidal module labeled 'FLAME recon', which reconstructs a 3D facial mesh. The output mesh is displayed on the right, along with a side view showing facial markers (blue dots) and a front view with a green vertical line indicating symmetry and an orange arc indicating mouth convexity. These features are used to compute various loss terms during training.

A dashed green box encloses the loss computation section, labeled 'E_loss'. Inside this box, three types of loss are computed: 'geometry' (from the reconstructed mesh), 'asymmetry' (based on the vertical alignment of markers), and 'mouth convexity' (based on the curvature of the lower lip). These losses are backpropagated to update the parameters of the 'code difference predictor' during training.

During testing, the dashed lines are not active, meaning the loss computation is bypassed, and the predicted code is directly used to generate the final reconstructed mesh without feedback. The figure also includes a dashed green arrow from the 'latent code' to the 'E_loss' box, indicating that the original latent code is also used in loss computation during training, likely for comparison or regularization purposes.

All modules are connected with solid black arrows indicating forward data flow, while dashed green arrows indicate feedback paths or auxiliary connections for loss computation. The visual design uses distinct colors and shapes to differentiate between data representations (cylinders), processing modules (trapezoids and rectangles), and loss components (dashed box).
